newsitem.title: RWANDA: U.N. agency asks Rwanda authorities for protection.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency asks Rwanda authorities for protection.

text.p: The U.N. human rights agency asked Rwandan authorities on Wednesday to protect its operations after gunmen killed four of its monitors in the latest in a wave of attacks.

Heads of U.N. agencies in Rwanda discussed how to respond to the increasing violence, putting at risk their help to rebuild Rwanda from its 1994 genocide. There have been eight attacks on expatriates in Rwanda in the last three weeks.
Following their meeting, U.N. officials said the government would issue a statement later on the status of U.N. operations.
The U.N. Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda (HRFOR) said in a statement it had asked "Rwandan authorities to investigate and take measures to increase the security of its operations."
The bodies of British and Cambodian monitors killed in the Tuesday ambush were flown to the capital from the southwest town of Cyangugu and were to be flown to Nairobi later on Wednesday.
HRFOR identified the two as 36-year-old Graham Turnbull of Britain and 34-year-old Saspra Chim Chan of Cambodia.

Two other monitors -- both Rwandans -- were killed with them on a visit in a marked U.N. vehicle to Karengera commune in the southwest, bordering on Zaire. Their Rwandan driver was wounded in the stomach and died during surgery.
After the killings, human rights monitors in Cyangugu and the western prefecture of Kibuye were pulled back to Kigali.
Security fears forced monitors in the northwestern provinces of Ruhengeri and Gisenyi back to the capital after the killing in cold blood of three Spanish aid workers on January 18.
A 61-year-old Canadian missionary was killed by a lone gunman on Sunday while giving communion at his parish church in a village 20 km (12 miles) north of Ruhengeri.
Claude Dusaidi, an adviser to Vice-President and Defence Minister Major-General Paul Kagame, said he was disgusted "at the actions of these thugs"
"In the meantime I don't think the United Nations should suspend operations in any of these areas," he told Reuters.

"What the United Nations should do to assist us in finding these people and controlling them is to give us (the government) more funds and more help. We need this for security purposes -- radios, communications and fighting equipment," Dusaidi said.
"It would mean we could have more gendarmes, more communal police and be in more places. These people are criminals. I do think they will come back and it could happen again," he said.
U.N. officials said they were investigating the ambush and few details were available.

But Dusaidi said government ministers may have been the targets because they were in the area on one of their tours to reconcile the Hutu majority and Tutsi minority in the wake of the return from Zaire and Tanzania last year of more than one million Hutu refugees.
The Hutus fled in 1994 during civil war fearing reprisals for the three-month mass slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he was "shocked and dismayed" at the killings. There are 139 U.N. human rights officers in Rwanda and it was the first loss of life from an attack on their operation to monitor rights abuses.
They reported on Friday Hutu death squads were killing Tutsi genocide survivors and witnesses to the slaughter, apparently to stop them denouncing people for the 1994 ethnic bloodbath.
